flashcards.q: What is the correct order for an EDA process and why does the order matter?
flashcards.a: 1) Grain & shape 2) per-column univariate (dtype, missingness, skew, cardinality) 3) relationships between features (Pearson AND Spearman) 4) relationship to target (binned means, class balance) 5) leakage + imbalance hunt LAST. Order matters because you need stages 1-4 to know what 'normal' correlation/behavior looks like in this dataset before 'implausibly good' (leakage) means anything.

flashcards.q: Why does Pearson correlation miss a real relationship like y = x^3?
flashcards.a: Pearson's r measures the strength of a LINEAR fit only. A strictly monotonic but curved relationship like y=x^3 can produce a low Pearson r in some ranges even though x fully determines y, because a straight line fits a cubic curve poorly even when direction never reverses.

flashcards.q: How does Spearman correlation fix Pearson's blind spot, and what does it still miss?
flashcards.a: Spearman replaces raw values with ranks before correlating, so any monotonic transform of x leaves rank order unchanged and Spearman reports the true strength of the monotonic dependency. It still misses non-monotonic relationships (U-shapes) -- both Pearson and Spearman report weak correlation despite a strong U-shaped relationship; that needs a scatterplot or binned analysis.

flashcards.q: Why does z-score outlier detection fail specifically on skewed data?
flashcards.a: Both mean and std used by z-score are sensitive to skew: the mean is pulled toward the long tail, and the std is inflated by the tail values. Result: real large values in the tail can fail to trigger the threshold (std already inflated by other tail points), while smaller values on the short side get over-flagged relative to a shifted mean.

flashcards.q: Why is IQR-based outlier detection more robust than z-score on skewed data?
flashcards.a: IQR uses the median and quartiles, which have a bounded influence function -- moving the single most extreme point in a dataset arbitrarily far doesn't move the median or quartiles at all, whereas it moves the mean and std substantially. That's the formal definition of robustness against exactly the corruption z-score is vulnerable to.

flashcards.q: What do Anscombe's Quartet and the Datasaurus Dozen prove, and what practical rule follows?
flashcards.a: Multiple visually completely different datasets can share identical mean, variance, and Pearson correlation to several decimal places. Practical rule: never trust a correlation coefficient or summary statistic without plotting the underlying scatter for any pair your summary stats flag as noteworthy.

flashcards.q: Give a concrete example of target leakage and explain why correlation alone doesn't catch it.
flashcards.a: Predicting loan default with days_since_last_payment, which is null for accounts in good standing -- the feature's EXISTENCE pattern alone encodes the outcome. Correlation alone doesn't catch it because a leak can be partial (encoding an intermediate variable, not the label directly) and still meaningfully inflate metrics without triggering a too-good-to-be-true correlation threshold. The only real test: could this value exist, in this exact form, at prediction time?

flashcards.q: Why is accuracy meaningless under a 99.5%/0.5% class imbalance, and what should you use instead?
flashcards.a: A constant 'always predict majority' classifier scores 99.5% accuracy. Use PR-AUC, F1, or recall-at-fixed-precision instead -- and note that even plain ROC-AUC can look deceptively good under extreme imbalance, so PR-AUC is generally preferred.

flashcards.q: You compute both Pearson and Spearman for a feature pair: Spearman=0.85, Pearson=0.15. What's your next step?
flashcards.a: Plot the scatterplot immediately -- a large Spearman-minus-Pearson gap is close to a direct signature of a monotonic-but-nonlinear relationship (curve, threshold, log/power-like) OR of a single influential outlier dragging the linear fit while rank-based Spearman stays robust to it. Distinguish by looking at the plot.

flashcards.q: Why can't a normal train/test split evaluation catch train-serving skew?
flashcards.a: A train/test split from the same historical snapshot can't detect that the world has moved on since collection -- a model can have excellent, honest offline test performance and still degrade in production purely from feature distribution shift between training-data collection and live serving. You must compare training data distributions against CURRENT production data directly (e.g. sweetviz comparison reports).

flashcards.q: When should you NOT drop IQR-flagged outlier points?
flashcards.a: When they correlate with the target -- in fraud, medical, and safety-critical domains, IQR/z-score-flagged 'outliers' are frequently the exact minority-class examples the model exists to detect. Cross-reference flagged outliers against the target before removing them.

flashcards.q: What is the modified z-score and why is it more robust than the standard z-score?
flashcards.a: 0.6745 * (x - median) / MAD (median absolute deviation), commonly thresholded at 3.5. It's robust because both median and MAD have bounded influence functions, unlike mean and std, giving a z-score-shaped statistic without sensitivity to the outliers it's trying to detect.

flashcards.q: How do you scale EDA down for a 500-column, 50-million-row dataset?
flashcards.a: Sample rows first (compute cost scales with rows far more than statistical precision does past a certain sample size), then use a cheap full-column pass (single tree model importances or per-column mutual information) to shortlist plausible predictors before running expensive O(p^2) pairwise correlation on the full column set.
